body:
His personal devotion and his support for Buddhism

Harsha's religious life cannot be described accurately with only one label. His inscriptions call him Paramamaheshvara, meaning a devoted worshipper of Shiva. At the same time, his reign became known for substantial support to Buddhism, particularly the Mahayana tradition, and for his respect for other religious groups.

Mahayana is a major Buddhist tradition that gives importance to the ideal of the bodhisattva—a being devoted to enlightenment and the welfare of others. Xuanzang's presence at court strengthened the association between Harsha and Mahayana learning. Evidence of his devotion to Shiva and his later Buddhist patronage can coexist; support for Buddhism does not establish that he ceased to honour Shiva or the Sun.

Religious and educational benefactions

Harsha supported Nalanda and Buddhist religious establishments and made charitable gifts to religious specialists and people in need. During his Prayag gathering, observances honoured the Buddha, the Sun and Shiva on successive days. Gifts went to Buddhists, Brahmins and the poor. This is a clear example of the difference between a ruler's personal devotional preference and the groups that received royal patronage.

A king and a court associated with Sanskrit learning

Harsha is traditionally credited with 3 Sanskrit plays:

  • Ratnavali—a courtly drama.
  • Priyadarshika—another courtly drama.
  • Nagananda—a play centred on self-sacrifice and associated with Buddhist ethical themes.

The Sanskrit author Banabhatta was a poet at Harsha's court. His best-known works include Harshacharita, the life of Harsha, and Kadambari, a prose romance. The distinction is straightforward: Harshacharita and Kadambari are works of Bana; the 3 plays are attributed to Harsha.

Calling Harsha only a “Buddhist ruler” overlooks his Shaiva titles and broader gifts. Calling him only a “Shaiva ruler” overlooks his prominent Mahayana patronage. Both types of evidence are relevant.

Prelims focus

  • Paramamaheshvara: title identifying devotion to Shiva.
  • Harsha was an important supporter of Mahayana Buddhism.
  • At Prayag, the Buddha, Sun and Shiva were honoured.
  • Plays attributed to Harsha: Ratnavali, Priyadarshika, Nagananda.
  • Banabhatta: Harshacharita and Kadambari.
  • Trap: The writer of Harshacharita was not the writer traditionally credited with Nagananda.

[IGNOU, History of Bharat: From the Earliest Times to 700 CE, Unit 13 “The Vardhana Dynasty,” §13.7.1, pp. 259–260 (accessed 18 November 2026); P. Bhaskar Reddy, “Harshavardhana,” Outlines of Indian History, INFLIBNET, §§8 and 10, consulted 18 November 2026; NCERT, Our Pasts–I, Class 6, ch. 11, p. 114 (2018–19 edition).]

pictures.alt: Harsha’s recorded devotion to Shiva coexisted with support for Mahayana and Nalanda, Prayag observances, and gifts to diverse recipients.
pictures.caption: Harsha’s devotion and patronage were not identical.

title: Harsha’s religious patronage and Sanskrit literature

body:
The Kannauj assembly: Mahayana teaching

In 643 CE, Harsha convened an important religious gathering at Kannauj in honour of Xuanzang. The assembly brought together rulers, Buddhist monks and representatives of other religious traditions. Mahayana Buddhist teaching and discussion occupied a prominent place; Xuanzang was the leading scholar associated with its proceedings.

This was a special gathering associated with Xuanzang, not an assembly whose defining feature was repetition every 5 years. Its connection with Harsha's Buddhist interests should not be confused with the purpose of the Prayag charitable distribution.

The Prayag assembly: recurring charity

Harsha also held a major assembly at Prayag (present-day Prayagraj), at the meeting of the Ganga and Yamuna rivers. The gathering is commonly called the Mahamoksha assembly. Its defining feature was the distribution of wealth and gifts at 5-year intervals. Xuanzang attended one such assembly after the Kannauj gathering.

At Prayag, the observances included homage to the Buddha, the Sun and Shiva. Harsha distributed gifts among Buddhist monks, Brahmins, religious practitioners and needy people. The event therefore demonstrates charity across religious communities, rather than an exclusive attempt to promote Mahayana Buddhism.

Keep the 2 gatherings separate

FeatureKannaujPrayag
Key associationXuanzang and Mahayana discussionRecurring distribution of charity
TimingSpecial gathering in 643 CEHeld every 5 years
PlaceKannauj, Uttar PradeshGanga–Yamuna confluence
Religious characterMahayana emphasis, with varied attendeesGifts and observances involving several traditions

Kannauj = Xuanzang and Mahayana discussion. Prayag = every 5 years and broad charity. Xuanzang was associated with both, so his presence alone does not identify which assembly is being described.

Harsha in one view

Harsha's career connects the Vardhana family of Thanesar with Kannauj, eastern alliances and opposition, a southern limit at the Narmada, regional officers and samantas, Xuanzang and Nalanda, and public religious patronage. These connections explain why he was a prominent northern Indian ruler without suggesting that he conquered the entire subcontinent.

Prelims focus

  • Kannauj gathering: 643 CE, held in Xuanzang's honour.
  • Kannauj: associated especially with Mahayana Buddhist discussion.
  • Prayag: at the Ganga–Yamuna confluence.
  • Prayag's charitable assembly recurred every 5 years.
  • Prayag gifts went to people of several religious traditions and to the poor.
  • Trap: The 5-year interval belongs to Prayag, not to the special Kannauj gathering.

[P. Bhaskar Reddy, “Harshavardhana,” Outlines of Indian History, INFLIBNET, §§8.1–8.2, consulted 18 November 2026; IGNOU, History of Bharat: From the Earliest Times to 700 CE, Unit 13, §§13.7.2–13.7.3, pp. 260–261, accessed 18 November 2026; IGNOU, History of India from c. 300 C.E. to 1206, BHIC-132, Unit 3, pp. 39–42 (2019).]
